bull.b: Arm’s dual revenue streams—upfront licensing plus usage-based royalties—create durable, scalable cash flows tied to chip shipments. Broad platform adoption and a large developer ecosystem increase switching costs and sustain recurring high-margin revenue as semiconductor adoption grows across end markets.

Very low leverage and expanding equity provide financial flexibility to invest in R&D, secure supply, and support a silicon initiative without relying on external financing. Recent FCF strength lets management fund operating investments and capital-intensive ramps while absorbing cyclical headwinds.

bull.t: Data Center Momentum & AGI CPU Traction
bull.b: Rapid adoption in data center infrastructure and strong AGI CPU demand materially expand Arm’s TAM beyond mobile. Customer wins and faster Neoverse shipments validate ecosystem shift to Arm, positioning the company to capture long-term higher-value silicon and royalty pools as AI compute proliferates.

bear.b: Arm’s silicon opportunity depends on third-party foundry and assembly/test capacity; persistent wafer, substrate and memory bottlenecks can cap AGI CPU shipment rates. These external constraints could push meaningful revenue and margin upside into FY29–FY30, slowing realization of projected growth.

Historic swings in operating and EBITDA margins reflect sensitivity to product mix, R&D timing, and new silicon economics. Transitioning to silicon (initial lower AGI CPU margins) plus elevated op-ex increases the risk that near-term profitability and cash conversion remain uneven over the medium term.

Arm still earns meaningful royalties tied to handset volumes; handset demand softness and higher BOM costs can restrain royalty growth. Because royalties scale with end-market unit cycles, handset volatility can produce lumpy revenue and temper overall royalty growth even as data-center adoption improves.
